abstract.t: This document describes how to integrate multiple OAuth 2.0 extensions to enable secure authorization for AI agents acting on behalf of users. It combines cross-domain identity, policy-based authorization, user consent evidence, and multi-hop delegation into a cohesive framework for autonomous agent authorization.

section.title: Introduction
section.t: AI agents increasingly need to access protected resources on behalf of users across different trust domains. Traditional OAuth 2.0 provides basic delegation mechanisms, but AI agent scenarios require additional capabilities:

ul.li: Cross-domain user identity verification;
Fine-grained, policy-based authorization;
Verifiable user consent evidence;
Secure multi-agent delegation chains.

section.t: This document describes how to combine several OAuth 2.0 extensions into an integrated framework for AI agent authorization. It does not define new protocol mechanisms, but rather profiles existing specifications for this use case.
Two key design principles guide this framework:

ul.li: Progressive Deployment: Organizations can adopt AOA capabilities gradually through a two-dimensional deployment matrix, starting with simple configurations and upgrading to full runtime authorization as requirements evolve (see ).

Reverse-Guided Authorization: Resource servers can guide agents toward appropriate authorization by returning structured error responses that specify required policies and constraints, enabling AI agents to adaptively construct valid authorization requests (see ).

section.title: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals.

tr.td: User consent via JWT grant interaction flow

section.title: Authorization Model: Policy vs Scope
section.t: AOA uses a policy-based authorization model that replaces traditional OAuth 2.0 scopes with fine-grained Rego policies. This section clarifies the relationship between scopes and policies in AOA.

section.title: Rego Policy as Primary Authorization Mechanism
section.t: In AOA, the primary authorization mechanism is Rego policy carried via Rich Authorization Requests (RAR, ), not OAuth 2.0 scopes. The rego_policy authorization data type defined in carries the authorization logic within the authorization_details parameter:

ul.li: Authorization Request: Clients submit authorization_details containing a rego_policy type with Rego policy that defines permitted operations (e.g., "allow add_to_cart if amount <= 50").
Access Token: AS returns an enriched authorization_details response per RFC 9396 Section 7.1, including the evaluated policy reference.
Resource Server: RS evaluates the policy at runtime using a Rego-compatible policy engine with request context.

section.t: This approach enables dynamic, context-aware authorization that goes beyond static scope lists.

section.title: Scope as Optional Supplement
section.t: Traditional OAuth 2.0 scope parameter is OPTIONAL in AOA and serves different purposes:

ul.li: When to use scope: For coarse-grained resource categorization (e.g., "read", "write") or backward compatibility with existing OAuth deployments.
When NOT to use scope: When fine-grained, conditional authorization is required. In this case, Rego policy provides all necessary authorization logic.
Relationship: If both scope and policy are present, the policy takes precedence. Scope acts as an outer boundary, while policy defines specific conditions.

section.title: Complete Authorization Mechanism
section.t: AOA's complete authorization mechanism comprises four integrated components:

ol.li: Cross-Domain Identity (): Proves "who the user is" across trust domains via JWT assertion.
Consent Evidence (): Provides cryptographic proof of "what the user agreed to".
Chain Delegation (): Enables secure "agent-to-agent transfer" of authorization.
Rego Policy (): Defines "what operations are allowed" with fine-grained conditions.

section.t: Together, these components provide end-to-end authorization for AI agents:

dl.dd: Authenticates the user and issues ID Tokens. This is the user's trusted identity service.
An autonomous software agent acting on behalf of the user. Has its own workload identity (SPIFFE/WIT-SVID).
Issues access tokens for resources in its domain. Validates JWT assertions, evaluates authorization_details, and manages user interaction.
Hosts protected resources. Validates access tokens and enforces policies using a Rego-compatible policy engine.

section.title: Token Structure
section.t: The framework uses JWT access tokens following OAuth 2.0 standards. Key claim semantics:

ul.li: sub (Subject): MUST contain the user's identifier at the Resource Application (third-party app), NOT the Agent's internal user identifier. This enables the Resource Server to immediately identify the resource owner without additional identity mapping lookups. The AS extracts this value from the JWT assertion's subject claims.

li.t: act (Actor): Identifies the entity exercising delegated authority. Contains:

ul.li: sub: The Agent's WIT URI, identifying which agent is acting on behalf of the user;
agent_user_id (OPTIONAL): The user's identifier at the Agent system, enabling audit trail correlation at the Agent side. Note: This is a non-registered extension field within the act claim structure.

li.t: User Authentication at Agent: User authenticates with the Agent's Identity Provider (IdP). The Agent's IdP issues an ID Token containing:

ul.li: sub: The user's identifier at the Agent system (e.g., agent_user_001);
aud: The agent's SPIFFE ID, binding this token to the specific agent.

li.t: ID Token as JWT Assertion: The Agent uses the ID Token as the JWT assertion in the token request per . The AS validates the Home IdP's signature and extracts the user's identity claims.
Token Request Construction: Agent builds a token request including:

ul.li: grant_type: urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer;
assertion: The user's ID Token (JWT);
authorization_details: Containing rego_policy type with policy and context;
redirect_uri (OPTIONAL): For interaction completion notification.

li.t: Token Request Submission: Agent sends the token request to External AS with SPIFFE client authentication (WIT-SVID in headers).

ul.li: SPIFFE client credentials;
JWT assertion signature from Home IdP;
Policy syntax and safety in authorization_details.

li.t:
Interaction Required: AS determines user interaction is needed and returns an interaction_required error response per
containing an interaction_uri for user consent.
User Interaction: The agent launches the interaction_uri in the user's browser. The AS presents the consent UI showing the interpreted operation.
User Confirmation: User reviews and approves the operation.
Polling: Agent polls the token endpoint (re-sending its original request) until the AS completes user interaction.
Token Issuance: AS issues access token containing:

ul.li: act: Agent's SPIFFE ID;
authorization_details: Enriched response per RFC 9396 Section 7.1;
evidence: Signed user confirmation record.

li.t: API Request: Agent presents token to Resource Server.
Token Validation: RS validates token signature and claims.
Policy Evaluation: RS sends policy and request context to the policy engine.
Authorization Decision: Policy engine returns allow/deny decision.
Response: RS executes (or denies) the operation and returns response.

section.title: User Consent Modes
section.t: The framework supports multiple consent mechanisms:

section.title: Redirect-Based Consent
section.t: Traditional OAuth redirect flow where the agent redirects the user to the AS's consent page.

section.title: CIBA-Based Consent
section.t: Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication (CIBA) for out-of-band consent, useful when the agent cannot redirect the user.

section.title: Consent-Only Flow
section.t: When the user has a valid, non-expired ID Token and the agent's identity is already trusted, the AS MAY skip re-authentication and only prompt for consent to the specific operation.

section.title: Progressive Deployment
section.t: The AOA framework supports progressive deployment through a two-dimensional matrix, allowing organizations to adopt capabilities gradually based on their security requirements and operational maturity.

section.title: Identity Deployment Levels
section.t: Implementations MAY deploy agent identity at three progressive levels:

section.title: Level 0: Self-Issued Identity
section.t: The agent generates its own key pair and self-issues identity assertions. Suitable for development, testing, and low-trust scenarios such as personal or small-team agents.

section.title: Level 1: WIMSE Workload Identity
section.t: The agent obtains workload identity tokens through WIMSE infrastructure. Provides cross-domain verifiability without requiring full enterprise IdP deployment. This level can be enhanced with optional trusted execution environment verification using WIT Attestation.

section.title: Level 2: Enterprise Identity
section.t: The agent's identity is managed by an enterprise IdP with full X.509 or SAML/OIDC trust chains. Required for high-assurance enterprise deployments.

section.title: Token Deployment Levels
section.t: Authorization tokens can be deployed at three levels:

section.title: Level A: Pre-configured Tokens
section.t: Static tokens configured at deployment time. No runtime AS interaction required. Suitable for internal services and well-known agents.

section.title: Level B: Admin-Assigned Tokens
section.t: Tokens assigned by administrators through a management interface. Policy binding without end-user consent. Suitable for enterprise automation scenarios.

section.title: Level C: Runtime AOA Tokens
section.t: Full AOA flow with user consent, policy evaluation, and evidence recording. Required for high-sensitivity operations and cross-domain access. This level utilizes the JWT Grant Interaction Response mechanism for user consent.

section.t: The combination of identity and token levels creates a deployment matrix:
Organizations typically progress through the matrix as their requirements evolve, starting from lower levels (e.g., 0A) and upgrading to higher levels (e.g., 2C) based on security needs.

section.title: Reverse-Guided Authorization
section.t: Traditional OAuth error responses indicate authorization failure without guidance on how to obtain valid authorization. In AI agent scenarios, where agents may autonomously navigate authorization requirements, resource servers can provide structured guidance through error responses.
When an agent's request lacks sufficient authorization, the resource server returns a 403 Forbidden response with a rego_profile object that specifies:

ul.li: Required scopes or authorization details;
Policy constraints that must be satisfied;
Whether user consent is required;
Reference to the authorization server capable of issuing appropriate tokens.

section.t: The AI agent parses this guidance and constructs a new authorization request that satisfies the specified requirements. This enables agents to "learn" authorization requirements dynamically rather than requiring pre-programmed knowledge of each resource server's policies.
Detailed specification of the Rego Profile format and agent adaptive behavior is defined in .

section.title: Trust Boundaries
section.t: The framework establishes clear trust boundaries:

ul.li: Home IdP → Agent: ID Token with agent in audience;
Agent → External AS: SPIFFE authentication + JWT assertion (ID-JAG);
External AS → RS: Signed access token with policy reference;
Delegation: AS-signed delegation chain entries.

tr.td: JWT assertion audience binding (assertion.aud == AS identifier)
AS signature on each chain entry

section.title: LLM Threat Model
section.t: This framework assumes the agent implementation (including authorization logic) is trusted, while the Large Language Model (LLM) used to derive operations is NOT trusted. The policy-based authorization ensures:

ul.li: LLM cannot directly control authorization decisions;
All operations are bounded by user-approved policies;
Audit trails enable post-hoc verification.

section.title: Relationship to Other Specifications
section.t: This section clarifies the relationship between this framework and other OAuth 2.0 specifications. Understanding these relationships is essential for implementers to determine which specifications are required for their specific use cases.

section.title: Relationship to Identity Assertion Grant (ID-JAG)
section.t: This framework builds on the Identity Assertion Authorization Grant () as the base grant type for cross-domain identity assertion. ID-JAG enables AI agents to present a JWT assertion (e.g., an ID Token from the user's Home IdP) to an external authorization server as proof of user identity.
This framework extends ID-JAG with:

ul.li: RAR-based policy authorization via the rego_policy authorization data type in authorization_details;
Evidence recording of user consent decisions.

section.t: Implementations of this framework MUST implement ID-JAG as the base grant type.

section.title: Relationship to JWT Grant Interaction Response
section.t: The JWT Grant Interaction Response () defines an extension to the JWT Authorization Grant that enables an authorization server to indicate that user interaction is required. Instead of immediately returning an access token or error, the AS returns an interaction_uri where the user can provide consent, along with a polling interval.
This framework uses JWT Grant Interaction Response for:

ul.li: Obtaining explicit user consent for AI agent operations without requiring a traditional OAuth redirect flow;
Enabling the agent to launch a browser for user interaction and then poll for completion;
Supporting both polling-based and redirect-based notification of interaction completion.

section.t: Implementations MUST support JWT Grant Interaction Response for user consent in AI agent authorization scenarios.

section.title: Relationship to Token Exchange (RFC 8693)
section.t: This framework uses Token Exchange () as the base delegation mechanism and extends it with the delegation_chain claim for complete auditability. While RFC 8693 provides point-to-point token exchange, this framework enables end-to-end delegation chain tracking.
Key extensions:

ul.li: delegation_chain claim records all delegation hops with cryptographic signatures;
Policy subset validation ensures privilege escalation prevention across delegation hops;

section.t: Implementations SHOULD support RFC 8693 for token exchange operations and MAY implement the delegation chain extension for multi-hop scenarios.

section.title: Relationship to Transaction Tokens
section.t: Transaction Tokens () focus on short-lived service-to-service authorization in microservices architectures. This framework focuses on longer-lived user-to-agent delegation with explicit human consent.
Comparison:
The two specifications can be combined: AOA for initial user authorization, Transaction Tokens for subsequent service-to-service calls within the authorized scope.

section.title: Relationship to CIBA
section.t: This framework profiles the OpenID Connect Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication (CIBA) specification for out-of-band user consent. While CIBA focuses on user authentication, this framework uses it for authorization and consent collection.
CIBA is used in this framework for:

ul.li: Scenarios where the agent cannot redirect the user to a browser (e.g., voice assistants, IoT devices);
High-security scenarios requiring out-of-band consent verification;
Mobile scenarios where the user completes consent on a separate device.

section.t: The framework extends CIBA by adding policy presentation to the consent interface and evidence recording of the consent decision.

section.title: Relationship to Rich Authorization Requests (RAR)
section.t: This framework uses Rich Authorization Requests () as the mechanism for carrying Rego policy in authorization requests via the authorization_details parameter. The rego_policy authorization data type defined in enables fine-grained, policy-based authorization within the RAR framework.
RAR integration provides:

ul.li: A standardized container (authorization_details) for carrying Rego policy and evaluation context;
Enriched token responses (RFC 9396 Section 7.1) that include the evaluated policy in the access token;
Compatibility with other RAR types, enabling combined authorization scenarios.

section.t: Implementations MUST support RAR (RFC 9396) with the rego_policy authorization data type.

section.title: Relationship to SPIFFE Client Authentication
section.t: This framework uses OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication () for agent authentication. SPIFFE provides workload identity through WIT-SVID (Workload Identity Token with SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Document).
The relationship is:

ul.li: SPIFFE Client Auth proves "who the agent is" through cryptographic workload identity;
This framework proves "what the agent is allowed to do" through user consent and policy authorization;
Together, they provide complete agent identity and authorization.

section.t: Implementations MUST support SPIFFE Client Authentication for agent identification.
